segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: OK, Graham, so let’s check we both know what we’re supposed to be doing.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: OK.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: So, for the university’s open day, we have to plan a display on British life and literature in the mid-19th century.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: That’s right. But we’ll have some people to help us find the materials and set it up, remember – for the moment, we just need to plan it.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Good. So have you gathered who’s expected to come and see the display? Is it for the people studying English, or students from other departments? I’m not clear about it.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Nor me. That was how it used to be, but it didn’t attract many people, so this year it’s going to be part of an open day, to raise the university’s profile. It’ll be publicised in the city, to encourage people to come and find out something of what does on here ( / ). And it’s included in the information that’s sent to people who are considering applying to study here next year. ( / )

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Presumably some current students and lecturers will come?

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: I would imagine so, but we’ve been told to concentrate on the other categories of people.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Right. We don’t have to cover the whole range of 19th-century literature, do we?

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: No, it’s entirely up to us. I suggest just using Charles Dickens.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: That’s a good idea. Most people have heard of him, and have probably read some of his novels, or seen films based on them ( / ), so that’s a good lead-in to life in his time.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Exactly. And his novels show the awful conditions that most people had to live in, don’t they: he wanted to shock people into doing something about it. ( / )

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Did he do any campaigning, other than writing?

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Yes, he campaigned for education and other social reforms, and gave talks, but I’m inclined to ignore that and focus on the novels.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Yes, I agree. ————————–

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: OK, so now shall we think about a topic linked to each novel?

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Yes. I’ve printed out a list of Dicken’s novels in the order they were published, in the hope you’d agree to focus on him!

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: You’re lucky I did agree! Let’s have a look. OK, the first was The Pickwick Papers, published in 1836. It was very successful when it came out, wasn’t it, and was adapted for the theatre straight away.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: There’s an interesting point, though, that there’s a character who keeps falling asleep, and that medical condition was named after the book – Pickwickian Syndrome.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Oh, so why don’t we use that as the topic, and include some quotations from the novel?

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Right, Next is Oliver Twist. There’s a lot in the novel about poverty. But maybe something less obvious ...

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Well Oliver is taught how to steal, isn’t he? We could use that to illustrate the fact that very few children went to school, particularly not poor children, so they learnt in other ways.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Good idea. What’s next?

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Maybe Nicholas Nickleby. Actually he taught in a really cruel school, didn’t he?

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: That’s right. But there’s also the company of touring actors that Nicholas joins. We could do something on theatres and other amusements of the time. We don’t want only the bad things, do we?

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: OK.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: What about Martin Chuzzlewit? He goes to the USA, doesn’t he?

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Yes, and Dickens himself had been there a year before, and drew on his experience there in the novel.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: I wonder, though ... The main theme is selfishness, so we could do something on social justice? No, too general, let’s keep to your idea – I think it would work well.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: He wrote Bleak House next – that’s my favourite of his novels.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Yes, mine too. His satire of the legal system is pretty powerful.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: That’s true, but think about Esther, the heroine. As a child she lives with someone she doesn’t know is her aunt, who treats her very badly. Then she’s very happy living with her guardian, and he puts her in charge of the household. And at the end she gets married and her guardian gives her and her husband a house, where of course they’re very happy.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: Yes, I like that.

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: What shall we take next? Little Dorrit? Old Mr Dorrit has been in a debtors’ prison for years ...

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: So was Dicken’s father, wasn’t he?

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: That’s right.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: What about focusing on the part when Mr Dorrit inherits a fortune, and he starts pretending he’s always been rich?

segments.speaker: CATHY
segments.en: Good idea.

segments.speaker: GRAHAM
segments.en: OK, so next we need to think about what materials we want to illustrate each issue. That’s going to be quite hard.
